summary:
For our project we created a software that simulates our solar system with the data from JPL Horizons system, but most importantly our software calculates the trajectory of a rocket launched from a selected facility on Earth to the Moon and visualizes that path with the motion of the spacecraft, which is modeled after Saturn V.
Furthermore we calculate the conditions for the lunar landing site chosen by the user, which are, accessibility to the solar energy and the ability to communicate back to the launching facility. Both of which are affected by moon’s topography and Earth’s position. Also the landing sites can be picked from a prelisted special areas such as Apollo missions landings and can be compared with any other freely chosen landing spot.
Then we calculate fairly optimal trajectory of the rocket to that landing spot, accounting for accounting for Earth’s spinning motion, Earth’s equatorial bulge, gravitational pull on the rocket from the Earth, the Moon and The Sun and during the launch, simplified model of the atmosphere for air resistance.
details:
Lunar mission explorer is an interactive 3D Moon landing mission planner that allows anyone to design, simulate, and explore their own mission to the Moon.

How does it work?

First, users select a launch site on Earth from several available locations. Then,they choose their desired site on the Moon. They can either select a historical landing location, such as one of the Apollo mission sites, or choose any point on the lunar surface.

Once the locations are selected, the application runs a physics-based simulation of the entire mission. It calculates optimal launch windows and simulates every major stage of the journey, including rocket ascent, translunar injection, mid-course corrections, lunar orbit insertion, and an Apollo-style guided landing. The simulation also models fuel consumption, allowing users to see how changes in fuel levels affect the mission.

The entire journey is visualized in a realistically scaled 3D Solar System, using planetary positon data from NASA's JPL Horizons system.

To make the experience even more immersive, we also included detailed 3D models of the available launch sites on Earth, allowing users to explore the locations from which their missions begin.

After touchdown, the application analyzes the chosen landing site to determine when sunlight will be available for solar power and when a direct line of sight to the Earth-based ground station will allows radio communcation.

It also visualizes the surrounding lunar terrain, analyzes surface slopes, and ranks different combinations of launch sites and landing sites based on important mission factors, such as sunlight duration and communication availability.

Our main goal is to make lunar mission planning easier and more accessible. By combining realistic physics simulations, real scientifc data, and an intuative 3D interface, we allow anyone even without an aerospace engineering background, to explore and plan their own lunar mission.

For the frontend and 3D visualization, we used TypeScript,React,Three.js, and React Three Fiber

For the backend and scientific calculations we used Python with FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, SpiceyPy, and Rasterio. We also used Node.js and docker to support development and deployment

To make the simulation as realistic as possible, we integrated data from NASA JPL Horizons, LRO LOLA, LROC QuickMap, NASA Blue Marble, NASA Planetary Fact Sheets, the LROC Lunar Pits Atlas, the IAU/USGS Gazetteer of planetary nomeclature and other NASA lunar imagery and historical datasets.
